stated: Increase the Digital Services Tax on social media firms and other tech giants from 2% to 6%, with revenues contributing to funding mental health professionals in schools.

source.quote: Increasing the Digital Services Tax on social media firms and other tech giants from 2% to 6%.

bearing_set.reason: The policy explicitly earmarks increased DST revenue to fund mental health professionals in schools, directly expanding mental health access — an O3 indicator — for young people.
In-school mental health professionals reduce barriers to learning and can narrow the attainment gap for pupils with mental health needs, directly touching school standards and attainment indicators.

The DST falls on large global tech companies (incidence likely on wealthy shareholders or digital-advertising budgets), while the spending benefits all state-school pupils — particularly those who cannot afford private mental health services — creating a plausible redistributive, inequality-narrowing effect.

membership_note: Three genuine bearings: healthcare access (O3), educational attainment and the attainment gap (O7), and a redistributive incidence story (O14). O12 is left out because the policy is explicitly designed to match revenue to spending, making the net fiscal effect approximately neutral; O13 and O11 are left out because DST's effect on UK business investment or household take-home pay is too indirect to clear the non-negligible bar at this stage.
